title: Vanilla Bundt Cake with Glaze
summary: A tall, ridge-patterned vanilla cake finished with a simple pourable glaze.
equipment: stand mixer or electric hand whisk

ingredients.item: unsalted butter, softened (about 18°C), plus extra for the tin
fine sea salt or table salt

steps.title: Heat the oven
steps.text: Heat the oven to 165°C (145°C fan) for at least 20 minutes before baking, with a shelf in the lower-middle position. This tin holds a large volume of batter, so a fully heated oven is important for even baking right through to the centre.

steps.title: Prepare the tin thoroughly
steps.text: Brush soft butter (or a flavourless oil) into every ridge and groove of the tin, dust it all over with flour, then tip out the excess. A non-stick baking spray works even better if you have one, since butter can sometimes make the cake stick. A Bundt tin's decorative ridges are exactly where a cake is most likely to stick, so missing even a small section can tear the pattern when it's turned out.

steps.title: Cream the butter and sugar
steps.text: Beat the butter, sugar and salt for 4-5 minutes until pale and fluffy, then beat in the eggs one at a time, mixing well after each, followed by the vanilla. Adding the eggs individually keeps the mixture emulsified rather than curdled, holding on to the air worked in during creaming.

steps.title: Alternate dry and wet
steps.text: Whisk the flour, baking powder and bicarbonate of soda together, then add it to the butter mixture in three parts, alternating with the soured cream in two additions, starting and finishing with the flour; mix on low just until smooth. Starting and ending with the dry ingredients keeps the batter from splitting, while the soured cream adds moisture and a gentle tang without making it too loose to hold its ridged shape.

steps.title: Fill and settle the batter
steps.text: Spoon the batter into the tin, level it off, then tap the tin firmly on the worktop a few times. Tapping settles the thick batter into every groove and knocks out large air pockets that would otherwise show up as holes once baked.

steps.title: Bake until golden
steps.text: Bake for 55-65 minutes, until the top is golden, it springs back when pressed, and a skewer pushed into the thickest part comes out clean. Because the central tube means no part of the batter is ever far from the hot tin, this shape bakes a large cake evenly without the centre lagging behind.

steps.title: Cool, then turn out
steps.text: Leave the cake in the tin for 10 minutes — long enough to firm up, but not so long that it starts to stick as it cools — then invert it onto a wire rack and leave to cool completely. Turning it out at that point catches the moment it has set but hasn't yet gripped the tin again.

steps.title: Glaze and serve
steps.text: Whisk the icing sugar, milk and vanilla together to a thick but pourable glaze, then spoon it over the top of the cooled cake so it runs down into the ridges. Waiting until the cake is fully cool means the glaze sets into a defined coating instead of melting into the crumb.

tips: Grease every ridge of the tin, right into the grooves, then dust with flour — missing even a small section is the most common reason a Bundt cake sticks and tears on turning out.
Tap the filled tin on the worktop before baking to settle the batter into every groove and release trapped air.
Turn the cake out after the full 10 minutes, not sooner or later — too soon and it's still fragile, too late and it starts to stick as it cools.
Let the cake cool completely before glazing, or the glaze will melt into the warm crumb instead of sitting on top.
safety: Don't taste the raw dough or batter: raw flour and raw egg aren't safe to eat until baked.
storage: Store under a cake dome or in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 4 days, or in the fridge for up to a week. Freeze un-glazed for up to 3 months, wrapped tightly, then glaze after thawing.
